question: Do prediction trajectories from many deep-network configurations occupy a common low-dimensional structure, and what does information-geometric compression actually establish about that structure?

key_findings.claim: The analysis represents a deterministic classifier on one fixed finite dataset as a product of per-example categorical predictions and compares models by mean Bhattacharyya dissimilarity.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 1 multiplies the N categorical output vectors, and Equation 2 reduces the negative log Bhattacharyya coefficient of the product to an average over samples. Appendix B obtains the factorization by conditioning on fixed weights and inputs and assuming independent label coordinates. This is a deliberately constructed empirical prediction space, not a stochastic joint law over the input domain; network outputs remain coupled through shared weights.

key_findings.claim: Progress and trajectory distance compare checkpoints after reparameterizing each run by projection onto the ignorance-to-truth Fisher geodesic.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 3 gives the square-root-sphere geodesic separately for each sample. Equation 4 projects a model onto the product-space geodesic to define progress, and Equation 5 integrates Bhattacharyya dissimilarity between equal-progress interpolants. Because the Bhattacharyya negative log coefficient can violate the triangle inequality, the resulting object is a trajectory dissimilarity rather than a guaranteed metric; Appendix D.2 also proves that progress can equal one despite substantial classification error.

anchors.section: Geodesics, progress, and trajectory comparison / Equations 3-5

key_findings.claim: InPCA exactly embeds the full finite dissimilarity matrix in a pseudo-Euclidean space, while the reported low dimension is a truncation score for centered pairwise dissimilarities rather than an intrinsic-manifold theorem.
key_findings.evidence: Equations 6-8 double-center the Bhattacharyya matrix, retain signed eigen-coordinates, and measure explained stress by Frobenius reconstruction. Theorem 1 in Appendix D proves that any finite symmetric zero-diagonal premetric has such an exact full-dimensional Minkowski embedding. Thus exact isometry is algebraic and generic; the empirical evidence is that this particular sampled matrix is compressible after sorting signed eigenmodes, not that the checkpoints form one smooth manifold of formally estimated intrinsic dimension. In truncated coordinates even squared Minkowski intervals can be negative, as the page-5 discussion notes for the truth point.

key_findings.claim: Across the retained CIFAR-10 checkpoint corpus, three InPCA coordinates preserve 76% of centered-distance stress and fifty preserve 98%; ImageNet gives 84% and 96%, respectively.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2 reports these train-set compression values for 151,407 CIFAR-10 checkpoints from 2,296 retained configurations and 792 ImageNet checkpoints. The CIFAR sweep began with 3,120 configurations and excluded numerical failures and runs that never trained beyond 90% error, leaving 824 configurations, or 26.4%, outside the main corpus. Figure S.1 shows that exclusions are uneven across architecture and optimizer, so the headline is conditional on the retained training runs rather than all attempted configurations.

anchors.section: Appendix C / retained configurations and Figure S.1

key_findings.claim: The test predictions are also compressible but are more diffuse and architecture-specific than the training predictions.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 5 reports 63% explained stress in three coordinates and 95% in fifty for CIFAR-10 test outputs, and the text emphasizes more distinctive architecture branches and differing endpoints. Appendix E.2 shows that random-label corner runs can approach the ordinary test trajectories mid-training but later diverge and finish with higher test error. This supports shared coarse structure while contradicting an unqualified assertion that all train and test trajectories traverse the same manifold.

anchors.section: Appendix E.2 / Figure S.11 and test branches

key_findings.claim: The joint train-test visualization is an approximate out-of-sample construction that depends on a one-to-one checkpoint correspondence and a self-averaging substitution.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 9 is the general new-point projection. Equation 10 then places test predictions in train-derived coordinates only because the train and test model lists have equal size and because a train-centered term is assumed close to its test counterpart. The paper calls this a peculiar trick; in ten dimensions it explains 0.52 of test pairwise distances versus 0.56 for a separately fitted test embedding.

anchors.section: Joint train-test embedding / Equation 10 and Figure 6

key_findings.claim: Subsampling gives strong train-set compression estimates, but the paper overstates fidelity for extremely small test subsets.
key_findings.evidence: The main text says the explained pairwise distance is consistently quite high even with very few samples. Figure S.3 supports stable low-dimensional scores for many subset sizes. However, Figure S.4 explicitly states that for test data the explained pairwise distance is low and the manifolds are more diffuse; its N=10 test panel visibly loses the original architecture geometry. The result is therefore a qualitative scaling heuristic, not uniform evidence that ten examples faithfully recover the test manifold.

key_findings.claim: Architecture is the strongest reported discriminator of equal-progress trajectories, but the associated significance analysis does not establish an independent-sample causal effect.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 7 and Figure S.9 cluster configuration-averaged trajectories and use random-forest permutation importance, with architecture ranked above optimizer, batch size, augmentation, and weight decay and p below 10^-6. Pairwise trajectory distances share endpoints/configurations and are dependent dyads; no grouped resampling, confidence interval, or held-out-architecture robustness analysis is reported. On ImageNet, architecture is also confounded with optimizer, horizon, augmentation, mixed precision, and label smoothing, so the broad conclusion is most credible as a controlled CIFAR-10 description.

anchors.section: Figure S.9 / test clustering and importance

key_findings.claim: Larger and smaller residual networks follow similar prediction-space paths, while the larger model advances faster under the paper's matched comparisons.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 7 and 9 show Small and Large ResNet trajectory clusters near one another and plot higher progress for the larger network at equal gradient-update counts on CIFAR-10 and equal epochs on ImageNet. This is evidence about two residual-network pairs and one progress coordinate; it does not identify why width/depth improves generalization or show that arbitrary model scales share identical paths.

key_findings.claim: Four reference distributions reproduce the dominant three-coordinate picture, but the interpretation is a structured approximation rather than a discovered three-dimensional state law.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 11 constructs two empirical progress-local arithmetic centroids in addition to ignorance and truth. Figures 10-11 show that the resulting three-dimensional basis aligns with the original InPCA view after Kabsch alignment, with RMSD 0.06 and similar explained pairwise distances for points filtered to Bhattacharyya distance below two. Because the centroids and progress are computed from the same corpus and three coordinates retain only 76% of train stress, the construction explains the leading visualization but leaves a substantial residual geometry.

key_findings.claim: Random-label and synthetic experiments support rapid convergence toward shared coarse trajectory structure, while also showing that low-dimensionality is not present in arbitrary checkpoint slices.
key_findings.evidence: After training AllCNNs toward random-label corners and switching to true CIFAR-10 labels, most train trajectories come within Bhattacharyya distance 0.15 of ordinary trajectories after progress 0.27 plus or minus 0.15, typically within three epochs. Synthetic five-class teacher tasks with sloppy and isotropic Gaussian inputs reach about 99% stress in ten dimensions. Yet Figure S.18 states that the initial and 0.5%-epoch collections across corner initializations are not low-dimensional, even though their complete trajectories compress. These experiments suggest a dynamical convergence phenomenon, not a universal low-dimensional slice of prediction space.

key_findings.claim: Metric and averaging variants confirm some coarse compression but materially change the geometry and downstream behavior.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix E.3 finds low-dimensional structure under intensive symmetric KL, product-geodesic distance, and ordinary PCA, but notes that PCA distorts the architecture/geodesic relations and IsKL stretches late training. Appendix E.4 evaluates six probability centroids for only one AllCNN configuration with thirty seeds; test errors range from 25.0% for the arithmetic mean to 18.9% for the harmonic mean, without uncertainty estimates. The main configuration averaging uses arithmetic means after only a preliminary similarity check, so centroid choice is not innocuous.

anchors.section: Appendix E.3 / Equations 15-16 and Figure S.12

key_findings.claim: The ImageNet initialization analysis exposes an uncorrected batch-normalization artifact in the collected checkpoints.
key_findings.evidence: With default PyTorch running statistics, randomly initialized ImageNet ResNet-50 models can start at 0.91 times the ignorance-to-truth distance. A few forward passes make them close to ignorance, but the paper says this repair was not applied to the collected ImageNet runs and therefore omits their first checkpoint. This is a concrete reproducibility and interpretation caveat for the common-initialization narrative.

anchors.section: Appendix C / batch-normalization initialization and Figure S.2

method.core_idea: Map every checkpoint's categorical predictions on a fixed sample set into one product probability space, compare all checkpoints by an intensive Bhattacharyya dissimilarity, and apply signed classical multidimensional scaling to visualize and compress the resulting finite geometry.
method.mechanism: Per-example output vectors are multiplied into a product distribution. Checkpoints are reparameterized by their projection onto the Fisher-geodesic from uniform ignorance to one-hot truth; linear interpolation between recorded checkpoints then supports equal-progress trajectory comparison. Double-centering and eigendecomposition of the pairwise dissimilarity matrix produce pseudo-Euclidean InPCA coordinates. Architecture clusters, subset projections, four-point reference embeddings, random-label corners, alternative divergences, and synthetic input spectra probe the observed structure.
assumptions: A fixed finite train or test sample defines the prediction space of interest.
Conditional label coordinates can be treated as independent after weights and inputs are fixed.
Mean negative-log Bhattacharyya overlap is a suitable intensive dissimilarity even though it is not a metric.
Linear interpolation in probability space between saved checkpoints adequately approximates each continuous training path.
Projection onto the ignorance-to-truth geodesic provides a meaningful common progress coordinate across architectures and optimizers.
Low-rank reconstruction of a centered dissimilarity matrix is evidence for an effectively low-dimensional manifold.
Arithmetic averaging over seeds/configurations preserves the trajectory geometry relevant to clustering.
Excluding numerical failures and configurations that remain above 90% training error does not invalidate conclusions about successful training trajectories.
The ImageNet subset and architecture-specific training recipes are representative enough for cross-architecture comparison.
The self-averaging term in the joint train-test projection is sufficiently similar between train and test predictions.

techniques.role: Places all checkpoints evaluated on the same finite samples in a common categorical product space.
Computes an intensive model-to-model dissimilarity from per-example probability overlaps.
Supplies the ignorance-to-truth reference curve in square-root probability coordinates.
Reparameterizes heterogeneous training runs by projection onto the reference geodesic.
Integrates checkpoint dissimilarity after equal-progress interpolation.
Embeds the centered dissimilarity matrix into signed pseudo-Euclidean coordinates.
Scores truncated reconstruction of the centered pairwise-dissimilarity geometry.
Adds unseen checkpoints or approximate test predictions to an existing embedding.
Ranks configuration variables by their ability to predict pairwise trajectory dissimilarities.
Tests whether trajectories initialized near random-label probability-simplex corners rejoin ordinary training paths.
Compares InPCA with symmetric KL, product-geodesic, and ordinary PCA embeddings.
Contrasts trajectory compression for isotropic and sloppy synthetic input covariances.

evaluations.baseline: The ambient product prediction space has N(C-1) coordinates, and the full signed embedding can use one coordinate per sampled model

limitations: Author-stated: only six CIFAR-10 architectures and three ImageNet architectures are evaluated, despite the broad wording about many deep networks.
The central Bhattacharyya quantity violates the triangle inequality, so prediction space and trajectory distance are not metric in the usual sense.
The exact pseudo-Euclidean embedding theorem applies to every finite symmetric zero-diagonal premetric and is not evidence by itself for a manifold.
Explained stress measures truncated reconstruction of a centered dissimilarity matrix, not local intrinsic dimension, smoothness, topology, or a generative manifold model.
Three coordinates leave 24% of CIFAR-10 train stress unexplained, and figure curves are hand-drawn guides rather than fitted manifold estimates.
The corpus excludes 824 of 3,120 attempted CIFAR-10 configurations, with architecture- and optimizer-dependent failure rates.
ImageNet comparisons confound architecture with optimizer, training horizon, augmentation, label smoothing, mixed precision, and other recipe differences.
The ImageNet training embedding uses only 50,000 of 1.28 million training images.
The joint train-test construction is approximate and requires equal ordered model lists plus a self-averaging assumption.
The pairwise random-forest analysis treats dependent trajectory dyads without a documented group-aware significance procedure.
Progress is empirically correlated with error but can equal one for a confident high-error classifier.
The synthetic and random-label experiments test narrow teacher tasks and a single AllCNN corner protocol rather than a broad causal mechanism.
Compression in fixed-sample prediction space does not imply that parameter optimization itself has low computational complexity.
The repository does not publish the full-precision distance matrices, raw outputs, or appendix data needed for an exact independent reconstruction.
failure_modes: Numerically unstable or persistently near-chance configurations are removed and therefore can fall outside the reported common structure.
Adam and large-batch SGD/Nesterov generate many early or late points far from the main train trajectory cloud.
Different architectures form visibly distinct branches, especially on test predictions.
Random-corner test trajectories can rejoin ordinary paths transiently and then diverge late in training.
Very small test subsets can produce diffuse embeddings that do not preserve the full-sample architecture geometry.
Signed coordinate truncation can yield negative squared Minkowski intervals and misleading Euclidean visual proximity.
Changing the divergence or using ordinary PCA changes architecture, geodesic, and late-training relationships.
Arithmetic averaging can leave the visible manifold and perform substantially worse than other probability centroids.
Default batch-normalization running statistics can place randomly initialized ImageNet ResNets far from uniform ignorance.
The public runner's default data and optimizer config paths do not exist, so an unmodified default invocation fails before training.
The documented S3 data prefix returns HTTP 403 as of the review date, preventing even the lower-precision plot-data path from being verified.
reusable_insights: Compare models in function or prediction space when parameter symmetries make weight-space distance uninterpretable.
Separate exact finite-distance embedding from empirical truncation quality and from claims about intrinsic manifold dimension.
A shared progress coordinate can reveal shape similarities that wall-clock time or epochs obscure, but its failure cases should be audited separately.
Report retention and exclusion by architecture and optimizer whenever a geometry claim is conditioned on successful training.
Treat pairwise model or trajectory observations as dependent and resample at the model/configuration level.
Metric, centroid, and sample-subset sensitivity are part of the scientific result rather than plotting choices.
Prediction-path compression is a descriptive phenomenon until a mechanism forecasts the geometry out of sample.
open_questions: Can a proper metric or divergence yield the same cross-architecture compression without pseudo-Euclidean negative directions?
What intrinsic-dimension, topology, or out-of-sample tests distinguish one smooth manifold from several intersecting low-rank branches?
Do excluded and persistently failing runs occupy separate reproducible structures rather than mere outliers?
Does architecture remain dominant under matched ImageNet recipes and group-aware statistical resampling?
Can the data spectrum, initialization distribution, and time horizon predict compression before training?
How do language models, generative models, sequence tasks, and reinforcement learning alter the prediction-space geometry?
Can the common-progress description generate a training intervention that improves speed or generalization?
Which probability centroid is geometrically and statistically appropriate for averaging trajectories?
How stable are the signed eigenspaces across datasets, sample subsets, and independent checkpoint corpora?
Can full raw predictions and exact distance matrices reproduce every reported panel from a clean environment?

competitive_landscape.title: Measuring the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes
competitive_landscape.difference: Li et al. define an operational parameter-space dimension by finding the smallest random subspace in which a model can be trained. The reviewed paper instead compresses already observed prediction trajectories; its explained stress is not the same intrinsic-dimension estimator and does not construct a trainable low-dimensional parameterization.

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient Descent Happens in a Tiny Subspace
competitive_landscape.difference: Gur-Ari, Roberts, and Dyer show that gradients align with a small Hessian-eigenvector subspace after early training. That is a parameter-gradient and curvature statement with a class-count prediction; the reviewed paper studies output probabilities across architectures and does not identify its axes with a Hessian subspace.

competitive_landscape.title: Large Scale Structure of Neural Network Loss Landscapes
competitive_landscape.difference: Fort and Jastrzebski propose high-dimensional connected loss-landscape wedges and demonstrate low-loss subspaces connecting multiple solutions. Their object is weight-space loss geometry and optimizer path selection; the reviewed paper avoids parameter correspondence and embeds finite prediction distributions instead.

competitive_landscape.title: Prevalence of Neural Collapse during the terminal phase of deep learning training
competitive_landscape.difference: Papyan, Han, and Donoho identify a highly structured terminal geometry of class means, classifiers, and within-class variability across common networks. Neural collapse is a representation and endpoint phenomenon with specific simplex predictions; the reviewed work spans complete probability trajectories and offers compression rather than the same terminal law.

competitive_landscape.title: A picture of the space of typical learnable tasks
competitive_landscape.difference: The same team already applies information geometry to low-dimensional manifolds of probabilistic models trained across supervised, meta-, semi-supervised, and contrastive tasks. The reviewed paper deepens the within-task, across-architecture trajectory analysis and adds random-corner and synthetic experiments; it does not originate the team's prediction-space manifold toolkit.

competitive_landscape.title: An Effective Gram Matrix Characterizes Generalization in Deep Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang and Chaudhari derive a differential equation for the generalization gap using contraction between training trajectories on perturbed datasets and an effective Gram matrix, then test loss predictions. This supplies a more mechanistic trajectory-to-generalization analysis, whereas the reviewed paper's common-manifold geometry is descriptive and uses fixed datasets.

competitive_landscape.title: An Analytical Characterization of Sloppiness in Neural Networks: Insights from Linear Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Griniasty and collaborators analytically decompose linear-model trajectory covariance and identify data-spectrum, initialization-scale, horizon, and stochastic-noise regimes controlling low-dimensional hyper-ribbons. It directly targets the reviewed empirical phenomenon, but only in linear squared-loss and fixed-kernel surrogates rather than the nonlinear prediction geometry measured here.

competitive_landscape.title: Trajectory-Restricted Optimization Conditions and Geometry-Aware Linear Convergence
competitive_landscape.difference: Chaudhry, Monod, and Yano replace ambient worst-case regularity with PL, error-bound, quadratic-growth, and Hoffman conditions restricted to the subsets actually traversed by an optimizer. Their theory makes convergence depend on visited geometry but does not establish that deep-network prediction paths are low-dimensional or estimate the InPCA structure.

competitive_landscape.title: Scalar Representations of Neural Network Training Dynamics
competitive_landscape.difference: Jimenez-Gonzalez, Soriano, and Lacasa encode parameter trajectories as temporal networks and test whether a scalar representation preserves Lyapunov and decorrelation behavior on one MNIST multilayer perceptron. It competes on extreme visualization compression, but its object, scale, and dynamical validation differ sharply from the reviewed cross-architecture prediction-space corpus.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim that many deep-network training processes traverse the same effectively low-dimensional manifold in prediction space, that architecture primarily distinguishes paths, that larger related networks follow the same path faster, and that far-separated initial predictions rapidly merge into the ordinary structure.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The exact 28-page v3 artifact analyzes more than 150,000 retained CIFAR-10 checkpoints and 792 ImageNet checkpoints with an information-geometric dissimilarity, signed InPCA, equal-progress trajectory comparison, train/test projections, configuration clustering, random-label corners, metric variants, and synthetic spectra. The main quantitative result is strong finite-matrix compression: 76%/98% train stress in 3/50 dimensions on CIFAR-10 and 84%/96% on ImageNet. Prior work already established parameter-space intrinsic dimension, tiny gradient/Hessian subspaces, neural collapse, connected loss geometry, and the same team's low-dimensional task-space information geometry. Later work supplies a linear spectral mechanism and trajectory-restricted optimization theory.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The paper's defensible novelty is the unusually broad checkpoint-scale empirical atlas of finite-sample prediction trajectories and its architecture/progress/corner probes. The strongest wording should be narrowed from one shared low-dimensional manifold to low-rank compressibility of a retained, metric-dependent checkpoint dissimilarity geometry with architecture-specific branches. Exact Minkowski embeddability is generic to any finite premetric; three-dimensional stress is incomplete; failures are selectively excluded; ImageNet recipes are confounded; and test/corner/metric results expose real departures. The work is therefore a valuable descriptive phenomenon and visualization framework, not a proof that deep optimization has low intrinsic computational complexity or a validated universal manifold law.

reviewer_notes: Read all 28 indexed pages of the exact cached arXiv v3 PDF, including the complete main text, references, notation, derivations, experimental setup, Equations 1-16, Theorem 1, Table S.1, and Figures 1-11 plus S.1-S.18; every rendered page and visual was inspected. The PDF and text hashes match the full-text index, all pages contain usable extracted text, and the current official arXiv record lists v3 revised 2024-03-19 and the PNAS 2024 journal reference. The artifact link resolves to grasp-lyrl/low-dimensional-deepnets at commit 86e1a18a51fe69aa9cbb7ad7154f41d57158b1cd (2024-03-31), with Apache-2.0 code, model/config modules, analysis scripts, plot notebooks, and large rendered notebook outputs. It has no environment lock, dependency manifest, CI, or tests; notebooks hard-code [local-artifact-root]/low-dimensional-deepnets; runner.py defaults to nonexistent cifar10-full.yaml and adam-200-0.001.yaml; no ImageNet training implementation is visible; and the README says full-precision distances, raw outputs, and appendix data are request-only. The advertised S3 prefix for lower-precision plot data returned HTTP 403 on 2026-08-24. No execution claim is made because the paper reports about 60,000 GPU-hours and the public artifact cannot reconstruct the exact source corpus. Competitor titles, scopes, dates, and versions were checked against current official arXiv records through 2026-08-24.
